canon.title: All canons, joined
canon.about: The union of 6 canons, glued along the beings, occasions and ties they share: Athens, 470–322 BC; Europe, 1785–1828; The European alliances, 1871–1914; Florence and Rome, 1401–1564; The Scientific Revolution, 1543–1727; Vienna, 1890–1938.

occasions.label: The Parthenon begun, in Pericles' programme of building, with Phidias overseeing the works
The panhellenic colony of Thurii founded under Pericles; Protagoras writes its laws
occasions.note: Protagoras's laws for Thurii rest on Heraclides Ponticus, cited by Diogenes Laertius (IX.50).

occasions.label: The Samian War: Sophocles among the generals with Pericles
Phidias's gold and ivory Athena Parthenos dedicated, at the Great Panathenaia
occasions.note: In the archonship of Theodorus, 438/437 (Philochorus); the Great Panathenaia fell in Hekatombaion, July-August.

occasions.label: Phidias prosecuted over the gold and ivory of the Athena, in an attack aimed at Pericles
occasions.note: Dated here by Philochorus, in the year of the dedication, 438/437, after which Phidias went to Elis; Plutarch puts it on the eve of the war, c. 432, and has him die in prison.

occasions.label: Anaxagoras prosecuted for impiety, defended by Pericles, leaves Athens for Lampsacus
occasions.note: Dated c. 433/432 by Plutarch's placing among the attacks on Pericles' friends, after the decree of Diopeithes; others put it in 437/436 or the 450s.

occasions.label: At the battle of Potidaea Socrates saves the wounded Alcibiades
At the City Dionysia Euripides' Medea is placed third, behind Euphorion and Sophocles
Pericles' funeral oration for the dead of the first year of the war
occasions.note: Winter 431/430; the words are Thucydides' (2.35-46).

occasions.label: In the plague and the invasion the Athenians depose and fine Pericles; they re-elect him soon after
occasions.note: In the second summer of the war, after the second invasion and the plague (Thucydides 2.59-65).

occasions.label: Protagoras praises the composure of Pericles at the deaths of his two sons
occasions.note: Protagoras fr. 9 DK, preserved in the Consolation to Apollonius ascribed to Plutarch.

occasions.label: Death of Pericles, of the plague
occasions.note: He outlived the outbreak of the war by two years and six months (Thucydides 2.65.6): autumn 429.

occasions.label: Death of Anaxagoras
Gorgias, on an embassy from Leontini, dazzles the Athenian assembly and wins an alliance
Aristophanes' Acharnians, with Euripides on stage lending rags, wins first prize
In the rout at Delium Socrates retreats steadily, Alcibiades on horseback beside him
Aristophanes' Clouds, with Socrates as a sophist in his thinkery, placed third
occasions.note: The text that survives is a partial revision of the play of 423.

occasions.label: Alcibiades elected general
Accused of profaning the Mysteries, Alcibiades is recalled from Sicily, flees to Sparta, and is condemned to death
Aristophanes' Thesmophoriazusae, a parody of Euripides and his plays
Plato, about twenty, becomes a follower of Socrates
occasions.note: Diogenes Laertius (III.5-6) has him burn his tragedies on hearing Socrates; the year is inferred from his age.

occasions.label: Alcibiades returns to Athens in triumph and is given command of all forces
occasions.note: On the day of the Plynteria, in Thargelion (Xenophon, Hellenica 1.4.12).

occasions.label: Death of Euripides at the court of Archelaus
occasions.note: In 407/406, before the Dionysia of 406. At the proagon of the next Dionysia Sophocles brought on his chorus in mourning (Life of Euripides).

occasions.label: After the defeat at Notium the Athenians remove Alcibiades from command; he withdraws to Thrace
occasions.note: Late 407 or early 406.

occasions.label: In the trial of the generals after Arginusae, Socrates, a prytanis, alone refuses to put the illegal motion
occasions.note: Autumn 406: the Apaturia, in Pyanepsion, fell during the proceedings (Xenophon, Hellenica 1.7.8).

occasions.label: Death of Sophocles
occasions.note: In 406/405, after the Dionysia of 406 and before the Frogs of 405 mourned him.

occasions.label: Aristophanes' Frogs wins first prize; its chorus mocks sitting idle by Socrates, chattering
Under the Thirty: Critias forbids Socrates to teach, Socrates refuses to arrest Leon of Salamis, and Plato, invited by his kinsmen to join them, is repelled
occasions.note: Plato's part rests on the Seventh Letter (324b-325a).

occasions.label: Alcibiades killed in Phrygia
Critias killed fighting the democrats at Munychia
Xenophon asks Socrates whether to join Cyrus; Socrates sends him to Delphi
occasions.note: Anabasis 3.1.5-7.

occasions.label: The trial of Socrates for impiety and corrupting the young; he names Aristophanes' comedy among the old slanders, and Plato offers surety for his fine
occasions.note: Apology 19c, 34a, 38b.

occasions.label: Death of Socrates by hemlock; Plato is absent, ill
occasions.note: Phaedo 59b.

occasions.label: Xenophon, an exile, fights with Agesilaus of Sparta against Athens and Thebes
occasions.note: Whether his exile was decreed in 399 or after Coronea is disputed.

occasions.label: Plato's first voyage to Sicily: he wins Dion and offends the elder Dionysius
occasions.note: The story that Dionysius had him sold as a slave (Diogenes Laertius III.18-20) is late and doubted.

occasions.label: Plato begins to teach in the grove of the Academy
occasions.note: The year, c. 387, is traditional.

occasions.label: Eudoxus comes to Athens with his pupils and joins the Academy's circle
occasions.note: Diogenes Laertius VIII.86-87; the date is inferred, and the later story that he led the Academy while Plato was in Sicily is contested.

occasions.label: Death of Dionysius I; his son Dionysius II succeeds
Aristotle, seventeen, joins the Academy, while Plato is away in Sicily
Plato's second voyage, at Dion's call, to make a philosopher of the young Dionysius II
Dionysius II banishes Dion and keeps Plato at court
Plato returns to the Academy, where Aristotle has been studying for two years
occasions.note: Aristotle's twenty years in the Academy (367-347) are well attested; his presence at this occasion is inferred from them.

occasions.label: Xenophon's son Gryllus falls at Mantinea fighting for Athens; Xenophon's exile is over
Plato's third voyage: he quarrels with Dionysius II over Dion and is held until Archytas obtains his release
occasions.note: Speusippus' presence rests on Plutarch (Dion 22).

occasions.label: Plato, back from Sicily, meets Dion at the Olympic games; Dion resolves on war
occasions.note: Seventh Letter 350b-c.

occasions.label: Aristotle's dialogue Gryllus, on rhetoric, against the school of Isocrates
occasions.note: Lost; known from Diogenes Laertius II.55 and Quintilian. Isocrates' pupil Cephisodorus answered Aristotle.

occasions.label: Dion sails from Zacynthus and takes Syracuse from Dionysius II
Dion murdered by Callippus, an Athenian of the Academy's circle
Demosthenes' First Philippic
occasions.note: The date, 351 or 349, is disputed.

occasions.label: Death of Plato; Speusippus succeeds him at the head of the Academy
occasions.note: In the archonship of Theophilus, 348/347 (Diogenes Laertius III.2).

occasions.label: Aristotle leaves Athens and the Academy, with Xenocrates, for the court of Hermias
occasions.note: Why he left is not known: Speusippus' succession and the hostility to Macedon after Olynthus fell (348) are the two explanations.

occasions.label: Demosthenes on the embassy to Philip; the Peace of Philocrates
occasions.note: The two embassies of 346, from the spring to the oaths at Pella in the summer.

occasions.label: Isocrates' Philippus calls on Philip to unite the Greeks against Persia
occasions.note: Written soon after the Peace of Philocrates.

occasions.label: Aristotle on Lesbos with Theophrastus: their studies of animals and plants
Philip calls Aristotle to teach Alexander, then thirteen
Demosthenes' Third Philippic
Hermias betrayed to the Persians and executed
occasions.note: Aristotle honoured him with a hymn and an epigram at Delphi.

occasions.label: Death of Speusippus; the Academy elects Xenocrates
Philip defeats Athens and Thebes at Chaeronea; Alexander leads the charge; Demosthenes fights in the ranks and flees
occasions.note: 7 Metageitnion (Plutarch, Camillus 19), about the beginning of August 338 BC.

occasions.label: Death of Isocrates, aged ninety-eight, days after Chaeronea
occasions.note: That he starved himself on the news of the battle is tradition.

occasions.label: Demosthenes chosen to speak over the dead of Chaeronea

Demosthenes appears garlanded in the assembly at the news, and mocks Alexander as a boy
occasions.note: Plutarch, Demosthenes 22; Aeschines, Against Ctesiphon 77 and 160.

occasions.label: Alexander visits Diogenes, who asks him to stand out of his sun
occasions.note: An anecdote (Plutarch, Alexander 14; Diogenes Laertius VI.38); its historicity is doubted.

occasions.label: Alexander destroys Thebes and demands the Athenian orators, Demosthenes first; Demades talks him round
Aristotle returns to Athens and teaches in the Lyceum, Theophrastus with him, as a rival to the Academy
On the Crown: the jury vindicates Demosthenes against Aeschines
After the death of Callisthenes, Aristotle's kinsman, Alexander writes that he will punish the sophist who sent him
occasions.note: Plutarch, Alexander 55.

occasions.label: Convicted of taking Harpalus' gold, Demosthenes is fined and escapes into exile
occasions.note: Harpalus came to Athens in 324; the Areopagus reported after six months, and the trials followed early in 323.

occasions.label: Death of Alexander, recorded by the Babylonian astronomers
occasions.note: 29 Aiaru: the evening of 10 or 11 June 323 BC.

occasions.label: In the revolt after Alexander's death Athens recalls Demosthenes from exile

occasions.note: His saying that he would not let Athens sin twice against philosophy is late tradition.

occasions.label: Death of Aristotle
occasions.note: In the archonship of Philocles, 322/321 (Apollodorus in Diogenes Laertius V.10), and so in the second half of 322 BC.

occasions.label: Hunted by Antipater's men, Demosthenes takes poison in the temple of Poseidon
occasions.note: 16 Pyanepsion, in October 322 BC.

The Saxon and Polish question settled: Prussia takes two fifths of Saxony
The powers declare Napoleon an outlaw
The Final Act of the Congress
Waterloo
The allies enter Paris again; Talleyrand heads the government
Canova recovers the Pope's works of art from the Louvre, with British support
The Holy Alliance
David, exiled as a regicide, leaves his studio to Gros
Rudolph enthroned archbishop; the Missa solemnis meant for it unfinished
Death of Napoleon
Death of Salieri
Death of Beethoven
Hegel visits Goethe
Death of Schubert
Wilhelm I proclaimed German Emperor in the Hall of Mirrors
The Treaty of Frankfurt: France cedes Alsace and most of Lorraine and pays an indemnity
The three emperors meet in Berlin
The League of the Three Emperors: the Schönbrunn convention of Russia and Austria-Hungary, which Germany joins
The War in Sight crisis: Russia and Britain warn Germany off a war on France; the tsar and Gorchakov in Berlin
occasions.note: Gorchakov's circular that peace was now assured humiliated Bismarck; how far Bismarck meant war is disputed.

occasions.label: Russia declares war on the Ottoman Empire
The Treaty of San Stefano, dictated to the Porte: a great Bulgaria under Russian protection
The Cyprus Convention: Britain guarantees the Porte's Asian lands against Russia and occupies Cyprus
The Congress of Berlin revises San Stefano: Bulgaria cut down, Bosnia to Austria-Hungary's occupation, Serbia independent
Alexander II's angry letter to Wilhelm I, the box on the ears
Wilhelm I meets Alexander II at Alexandrovo and makes peace with him
The Dual Alliance of Germany and Austria-Hungary, secret, against an attack by Russia
occasions.note: Wilhelm I ratified it only after Bismarck threatened to resign.

occasions.label: Alexander II assassinated; Alexander III succeeds
occasions.note: 1 March 1881 in the Julian calendar.

occasions.label: France imposes a protectorate on Tunis, which Italy had wanted
The Three Emperors' Alliance, secret, renewing the league
occasions.note: Giers, then running the foreign ministry for the aged Gorchakov, and Saburov were its Russian authors.

occasions.label: The Triple Alliance of Germany, Austria-Hungary and Italy, defensive above all against France
Britain defeats Urabi at Tel el-Kebir and occupies Egypt, an Ottoman province, France having declined to act with it
occasions.note: There was no war with the Porte, which protested and remained nominal suzerain; Egypt divided Britain and France until 1904.

occasions.label: The three emperors meet at Skierniewice, after the league's renewal in March
Serbia attacks Bulgaria and is beaten at Slivnitsa; Austria-Hungary halts the Bulgarian advance
occasions.note: Serbia had been Austria-Hungary's client since their secret treaty of 1881.

occasions.label: Alexander of Battenberg driven from the Bulgarian throne; Russia breaks with Bulgaria, Austria-Hungary resisting Russian control of it
The Triple Alliance renewed, with new promises to Italy
The first Mediterranean Agreement completed: Austria-Hungary adheres to the Anglo-Italian notes of 12 February
The Reinsurance Treaty of Germany and Russia, secret
occasions.note: Signed by Bismarck and Count Pavel Shuvalov.

occasions.label: Bismarck closes the Reichsbank to Russian bonds, the Lombardverbot
The second Mediterranean Agreement of Britain, Austria-Hungary and Italy, against Russian designs on Bulgaria and the Straits, urged on Salisbury by Bismarck
occasions.note: Bismarck's letter to Salisbury of 22 November 1887 is the act of Germany's here.

occasions.label: Wilhelm II succeeds; Bismarck stays chancellor
The first Russian loan floated in Paris
Wilhelm II forces Bismarck out; Caprivi chancellor
The Reinsurance Treaty lapses, Caprivi declining the renewal Giers asks for
The French squadron at Kronstadt, the tsar standing for the Marseillaise; the consultative pact of 27 August
The Franco-Russian military convention signed by the chiefs of staff, against the Triple Alliance
The military convention ratified by an exchange of notes
Bismarck in Berlin, reconciled with Wilhelm II
Caprivi dismissed
Alexander III dies; Nicholas II succeeds
occasions.note: 20 October 1894 in the Julian calendar.

occasions.label: The Triple Intervention: Russia, Germany and France make Japan give back the Liaodong peninsula
The Kruger telegram: Wilhelm II congratulates the Transvaal on repelling the Jameson Raid
Death of Bismarck
Fashoda: Kitchener meets Marchand on the Nile; France gives way
Delcassé in St Petersburg extends the Franco-Russian alliance
Queen Victoria dies, Wilhelm II at her bedside with the new king
The Anglo-Japanese Alliance, aimed at Russia in the Far East
The Triple Alliance renewed
The Prinetti-Barrère exchange: Italy promises France neutrality
occasions.note: The letters are variously dated, June to November 1902. Bülow had spoken in the Reichstag of Italy's extra dances.

occasions.label: Edward VII's visit to Paris
President Loubet and Delcassé in London; Delcassé and Lansdowne open the talks
Japan attacks the Russian fleet at Port Arthur: the Russo-Japanese War
The Entente Cordiale
The Dogger Bank incident: the Russian fleet fires on Hull trawlers; France mediates
Wilhelm II lands at Tangier: the first Moroccan crisis
Delcassé forced to resign under German pressure
Wilhelm II and Nicholas II sign a defensive alliance on the imperial yacht
occasions.note: Never ratified: Russia's ministers voided it, and Bülow offered his resignation over Wilhelm's amendment.

occasions.label: The Treaty of Portsmouth ends the Russo-Japanese War
The Algeciras conference: Germany isolated, with only Austria-Hungary at its side; Grey stands by France and allows military conversations
The Franco-Japanese agreement
The Russo-Japanese convention
The Anglo-Russian Convention on Persia, Afghanistan and Tibet
Edward VII meets Nicholas II at Reval
Edward VII visits Wilhelm II, who refuses any limit to his navy
Izvolsky and Aehrenthal bargain at Buchlau: Bosnia for the Straits
occasions.note: What was agreed is disputed; no minute was kept.

occasions.label: Austria-Hungary annexes Bosnia-Herzegovina
The Daily Telegraph interview, and Bülow's failure to defend the Kaiser before the Reichstag
Austria-Hungary indemnifies the Porte for Bosnia
Germany's démarche makes Russia accept the annexation; Serbia submits
Bülow resigns; Bethmann Hollweg chancellor
Nicholas II visits Edward VII at Cowes
Nicholas II visits Victor Emmanuel III: the secret Russo-Italian agreement of Racconigi
Death of Edward VII
Nicholas II and Sazonov at Potsdam: a German-Russian détente on Persia and the Baghdad railway
The second Moroccan crisis: the Panther at Agadir, the Mansion House speech, the Franco-German settlement
Italy declares war on the Ottoman Empire for Libya
The Serbo-Bulgarian treaty, under Russian patronage
Poincaré, prime minister, in Russia
The First Balkan War: the Porte at war with Serbia and Bulgaria
The Peace of Ouchy: the Porte cedes Libya to Italy
The Grey-Cambon letters: Britain and France to consult if either is threatened
The ambassadors' conference under Grey, to the Treaty of London: Albania made, Serbia kept from the Adriatic
The Second Balkan War: Bulgaria attacks Serbia and Greece, and the Ottomans retake Adrianople
The Treaty of Bucharest, imposed on Bulgaria
Pašić in Vienna sees Berchtold
Austria-Hungary's ultimatum makes Serbia leave northern Albania; Wilhelm II, in Vienna, approves
The Liman von Sanders affair: a German general to command at Constantinople; Russia protests
Wilhelm II visits Franz Ferdinand at Konopischt
Franz Ferdinand and his wife assassinated at Sarajevo
occasions.note: The assassins were Bosnian Serbs armed through Serbian officers of the Black Hand; how much the Serbian government knew is disputed.

occasions.label: The Hoyos mission: Wilhelm II and Bethmann promise Austria-Hungary support against Serbia
occasions.note: Franz Joseph's letter to Wilhelm II, carried by Hoyos from Berchtold's office, made the request.

occasions.label: Poincaré, now president, in St Petersburg with Viviani
Serbia's reply to the Austro-Hungarian ultimatum of 23 July; Austria-Hungary breaks relations; Russia stands by Serbia
Austria-Hungary declares war on Serbia
occasions.note: Berchtold put before the emperor a report of a Serbian attack at Temes-Kubin, which he struck from the declaration when it proved false.

occasions.label: Russia's general mobilization, ordered by Nicholas II at Sazonov's urging
occasions.note: 17 July 1914 in the Julian calendar.

occasions.label: Germany declares war on Russia
The secret alliance of Germany and the Ottoman Empire, against Russia
Italy declares its neutrality: Austria-Hungary's war is not the defensive case of the Triple Alliance
Grey tells Cambon that the British fleet will protect the French coasts
Germany declares war on France
Britain's ultimatum over Belgium expires: Britain at war with Germany
occasions.note: Bethmann's scrap of paper, to the British ambassador Goschen.

occasions.label: Austria-Hungary declares war on Russia
France and Britain declare war on Austria-Hungary
Japan, Britain's ally, declares war on Germany
After the Ottoman raid on Russia's Black Sea ports, Russia, Britain and France declare war on the Ottoman Empire
The Calimala's competition for the Baptistery's second doors: Ghiberti against Brunelleschi, each with a Sacrifice of Isaac
occasions.note: Ghiberti's Commentarii claim the palm outright; Manetti says the judges offered to share the commission and Brunelleschi refused. The panels were judged in 1402.

occasions.label: The Opera del Duomo's competition of models for the dome; Brunelleschi and Ghiberti among the competitors
Brunelleschi and Ghiberti appointed together to build the dome
occasions.note: With Battista d'Antonio; the dome was begun in August 1420. The month of the appointment is to be checked.

occasions.label: The Calimala commissions from Ghiberti the east doors, later the Gates of Paradise
occasions.note: 2 January 1424 in Florentine style; given here in the modern year.

occasions.label: Masaccio's Trinity in Santa Maria Novella, its painted architecture in Brunelleschi's manner
occasions.note: Brunelleschi's own part in the design is an attribution, not a document; Vasari says he taught Masaccio perspective.

occasions.label: Death of Masaccio in Rome, aged twenty-six
occasions.note: Vasari reports Brunelleschi's lament at the news.

occasions.label: Cosimo de' Medici arrested in the Palazzo della Signoria and exiled to Padua
Cosimo recalled from Venice; the Medici ascendancy begins
Alberti dedicates Della pittura to Brunelleschi, naming Donatello and Ghiberti beside him
occasions.note: The prologue also praises Luca della Robbia and Masaccio, then dead.

occasions.label: The competition for the lantern of the dome: Brunelleschi's model preferred to Ghiberti's and others'
Fra Angelico paints the altarpiece and the cells of San Marco, rebuilt at Cosimo's expense
Donatello's bronze David, made for the Medici
occasions.note: The date is disputed, from the 1430s to the 1460s; the statue stood in the Medici palace by 1469.

occasions.label: Death of Brunelleschi, buried in the cathedral by the Opera's leave
The Gates of Paradise set up at the Baptistery
Death of Fra Angelico in Rome
Cosimo gives Ficino a house at Careggi and Greek manuscripts of Plato to translate
Death of Cosimo de' Medici, Ficino reading Plato with him in his last days
occasions.note: Ficino's presence near the end rests on his own letter to Lorenzo.

occasions.label: Leonardo and Perugino in Verrocchio's workshop
occasions.note: Leonardo's apprenticeship is documented from the late 1460s; Perugino's there rests on Vasari. Giovanni Santi's rhymed chronicle (c. 1485) pairs them as two youths equal in age and in love.

occasions.label: Verrocchio's tomb of Piero and Giovanni de' Medici in San Lorenzo, for Lorenzo and Giuliano
Verrocchio's Baptism of Christ, an angel in it painted by Leonardo
occasions.note: Vasari's story that Verrocchio gave up painting on seeing the angel is not credited.

occasions.label: Lorenzo and Giuliano sell Verrocchio's bronze David to the Signoria
The Pazzi conspiracy: Giuliano killed and Lorenzo wounded at Mass in the cathedral; the Signoria hangs the conspirators; Sixtus IV stood behind the plot
occasions.note: Whether Sixtus IV consented to murder is contested: by Montesecco's confession he wanted the regime changed without bloodshed. War and interdict followed in June 1478.

occasions.label: Sixtus IV makes peace with Florence and absolves its envoys
Sixtus IV's contract with Botticelli, Ghirlandaio, Perugino and Cosimo Rosselli for the walls of the Sistine Chapel
Leonardo goes to Milan and offers Ludovico Sforza his services
occasions.note: The letter of offer survives in a copy; the Anonimo Gaddiano says Lorenzo sent him with a silver lyre. The year may be 1483.

occasions.label: Botticelli, Ghirlandaio and Perugino paint Lorenzo's villa at Spedaletto
occasions.note: Known from a Milanese agent's report on the painters of Florence (c. 1490), which names Filippino Lippi too; the frescoes are lost and their date is uncertain.

occasions.label: Ficino's Latin Plato printed, dedicated to Lorenzo; Pico arrives in Florence
occasions.note: That Pico arrived on the very day the Plato was published is Ficino's own story.

occasions.label: Death of Sixtus IV
Michelangelo apprenticed to Domenico and Davide Ghirlandaio for three years
occasions.note: Vasari prints the record from Ghirlandaio's book; Condivi passes over the apprenticeship. He stayed about a year.

occasions.label: Michelangelo, from the sculpture garden at San Marco, taken into Lorenzo's household
Savonarola returns to Florence, recalled with Lorenzo's consent at Pico's urging
Death of Lorenzo de' Medici at Careggi; Pico and Savonarola visit him
occasions.note: Poliziano's letter has Savonarola bless the dying man; a later Savonarolan life has him refuse absolution unless Lorenzo restored the city's liberty.

occasions.label: Death of Domenico Ghirlandaio
occasions.note: 11 January 1493 in Florentine style; given here in the modern year.

occasions.label: Piero de' Medici driven out; Savonarola, among the Signoria's envoys to Charles VIII, becomes the voice of the new republic
Death of Pico; Savonarola preaches at his burial in San Marco
Leonardo paints the Last Supper for Ludovico at Santa Maria delle Grazie
The bonfire of the vanities in the Piazza della Signoria
Alexander VI excommunicates Savonarola
Five citizens executed for plotting Piero de' Medici's return; Savonarola does not intervene for their appeal
The ordeal by fire fails; San Marco is stormed and Savonarola arrested by the Signoria
Savonarola hanged and burned in the Piazza della Signoria, papal commissioners present
Machiavelli elected Second Chancellor of the republic
Louis XII's army takes Milan; Ludovico flees, and Leonardo leaves the city
The Opera del Duomo and the Wool Guild commission the David
Cesare Borgia's patent names Leonardo his architect and general engineer
Machiavelli, Florence's envoy, at Cesare Borgia's court in Imola, where Leonardo draws his plan of the town
Cesare traps and kills his rebel captains at Senigallia; Machiavelli, with him, writes the account
Leonardo commissioned to paint the Battle of Anghiari in the hall of the Great Council
Machiavelli in Rome at the election of Julius II, who strips Cesare Borgia of the Romagna
Michelangelo taunts Leonardo in the street over the horse he never cast
occasions.note: An anecdote of the Anonimo Gaddiano, undated; placed here about 1504.

occasions.label: The committee on where to set the David: Leonardo, Botticelli and Perugino among its members
occasions.note: 25 January 1503 in Florentine style; given here in the modern year. Leonardo spoke for the Loggia dei Lanzi; the David went before the Palazzo della Signoria.

occasions.label: Leonardo's revised contract for the Anghiari, Machiavelli its witness
Michelangelo commissioned to paint the Battle of Cascina in the same hall as Leonardo's Anghiari
occasions.note: In the autumn of 1504; the month is approximate.

occasions.label: The David unveiled before the Palazzo della Signoria
occasions.note: Vasari's story of Soderini finding the nose too thick belongs here.

occasions.label: Julius II calls Michelangelo to Rome and commissions his tomb
Refused an audience, Michelangelo leaves Rome for Florence; the next day Julius lays the first stone of Bramante's St Peter's
occasions.note: Condivi blames Bramante's envy for turning the pope from the tomb.

occasions.label: Leonardo leaves for Milan on leave; Soderini protests that he has taken money and barely begun
Michelangelo, sent with Soderini's letters, submits to Julius II at Bologna and is given the pope's bronze statue to make
Michelangelo begins the Sistine ceiling for Julius II
occasions.note: Condivi says Bramante urged the commission in the hope that he would fail.

occasions.label: Raphael paints the Stanza della Segnatura for Julius II; Bramante portrayed in the School of Athens
occasions.note: Vasari says Bramante, his kinsman, brought Raphael to Rome and is the geometer of the School of Athens.

occasions.label: After the sack of Prato, Soderini deposed and exiled; the Medici return
Julius II says Vespers under the finished ceiling
Machiavelli dismissed from the chancery
Machiavelli, named in the Boscoli plot, imprisoned and tortured by the Medici regime
Death of Julius II
Giovanni de' Medici elected pope as Leo X; Machiavelli freed in the amnesty
Machiavelli tells Vettori he has written De principatibus, meant for a Medici
occasions.note: He hoped the Medici would employ him, even if they began by having him roll a stone.

occasions.label: Death of Bramante
Leo X names Raphael architect of St Peter's in Bramante's place
The Prince dedicated to Lorenzo di Piero de' Medici
occasions.note: The date of the dedication, and whether the book was ever presented, are uncertain.

occasions.label: Leonardo goes to France as Francis I's painter, lodged at Cloux
Cardinal Giulio de' Medici commissions Raphael's Transfiguration against Sebastiano's Raising of Lazarus, for which Michelangelo supplies drawings
Raphael's portrait of Leo X with Cardinals Giulio de' Medici and Luigi de' Rossi
occasions.note: Finished by September 1518, when it stood in for the pope at the wedding feast of Lorenzo di Piero de' Medici in Florence; the months are an estimate.

occasions.label: Michelangelo's contract with Leo X for the façade of San Lorenzo
Cardinal Giulio de' Medici commissions the New Sacristy of San Lorenzo, the Medici chapel
Death of Leonardo at Cloux
occasions.note: Vasari has him die in Francis I's arms; the court is documented elsewhere that week, and the story is not credited.

occasions.label: Leo X releases Michelangelo from the façade of San Lorenzo, to his bitter protest
Death of Raphael; the Transfiguration set at the head of his bier
Cardinal Giulio de' Medici, through the Studio, commissions Machiavelli's Florentine Histories
The imperial army sacks Rome; Clement VII besieged in Castel Sant'Angelo
occasions.note: The army was mutinous and unpaid; Charles did not order the sack.

occasions.label: The Medici expelled; the republic restored
Death of Machiavelli
The siege of Florence: the imperial army for Clement VII against the republic, Michelangelo in charge of its fortifications
occasions.note: Michelangelo was named governor of the fortifications on 6 April 1529, fled to Venice in September and returned in November. The siege ran from late October 1529; its end is the capitulation of August 1530. The coronation at Bologna fell within it, so the order of the two rests on the file.

occasions.label: Clement VII crowns Charles V emperor at Bologna
Florence capitulates; the Medici restored
Charles V makes Titian a Count Palatine and Knight of the Golden Spur
Michelangelo meets Clement VII; the Last Judgment probably first proposed
Death of Clement VII, two days after Michelangelo settles in Rome for good
The Last Judgment unveiled for Paul III
Titian in Rome at the Belvedere; Michelangelo and Vasari visit him, and Michelangelo praises his colour but regrets his drawing
Paul III makes Michelangelo architect of St Peter's
Titian at the imperial Diet paints Charles V at Mühlberg
Death of Paul III
Vasari's Lives printed by Torrentino, dedicated to Cosimo I, Michelangelo the one living artist in them; Michelangelo thanks him with a sonnet
Death of Charles V
Cosimo I in Rome, with Vasari, honours Michelangelo
The Accademia del Disegno founded at Vasari's urging, Cosimo I and Michelangelo its heads
occasions.note: 13 January 1562 in Florentine style; given here in the modern year. Michelangelo, in Rome, was elected in his absence.

occasions.label: Death of Michelangelo in Rome
occasions.note: 18 February 1563 in Florentine style; given here in the modern year. His body was taken secretly to Florence; the Academy's funeral in San Lorenzo (July 1564) and Vasari's second edition (1568), which ends with his Life, lie beyond this canon.

occasions.label: De revolutionibus orbium coelestium printed by Petreius, from the manuscript Rheticus brought from Frombork
occasions.note: Rheticus saw the first part through the press in 1542 and left for Leipzig; Osiander added the unsigned preface. The book was finished in the spring of 1543.

occasions.label: Death of Copernicus
occasions.note: That the printed book reached him on the day he died is a story first told by Tiedemann Giese.

occasions.label: Galileo thanks Kepler for the Mysterium cosmographicum and confesses himself a Copernican in private
Kepler arrives at Tycho's castle of Benátky
Kepler quarrels with Tycho over the terms of his employment, leaves in anger, and then apologises in writing
Tycho presents Kepler to the emperor, and the Rudolphine Tables are proposed in Rudolf's name
occasions.note: The month of the audience is not established; Tycho had been the emperor's mathematician since 1599.

occasions.label: Death of Tycho Brahe; Kepler records his last words, Ne frustra vixisse videar
Kepler appointed imperial mathematician in Tycho's place
Kepler's Astronomia nova, the first two laws, dedicated to Rudolf II
Sidereus nuncius, with the satellites of Jupiter named the Medicean stars for Cosimo II
Kepler's Dissertatio cum Nuncio sidereo, an open letter of support to Galileo
Galileo named Chief Mathematician and Philosopher to the Grand Duke
Galileo celebrated in Rome and enrolled in Cesi's Accademia dei Lincei
The dispute on floating bodies at the Grand Duke's table, where Cardinal Barberini takes Galileo's side
Death of Rudolf II
Galileo's Letters on Sunspots published by the Lincei
Bellarmine admonishes Galileo to abandon the Copernican opinion
occasions.note: Whether a stricter injunction, not to hold, teach or defend it in any way, was also served that day is disputed; the minute that says so was decisive in 1633.

occasions.label: The Congregation of the Index suspends De revolutionibus until it is corrected
occasions.note: The decree is certain; Bellarmine's part in the congregation's deliberation is to be checked.

occasions.label: Bellarmine gives Galileo a certificate that he has neither abjured nor been penanced
Death of Cosimo II
Il Saggiatore, published by the Lincei and dedicated to the new pope, Urban VIII
Galileo, after a stay with Cesi, has six audiences with Urban VIII, who allows a hypothetical treatment of the two systems
Descartes to Mersenne: the eternal truths are created by God
Death of Federico Cesi
The Dialogue on the Two Chief World Systems, with the pope's favourite argument in the mouth of Simplicio
Galileo before the Holy Office: interrogated from 12 April, sentenced and made to abjure on 22 June
occasions.note: Urban presided over the congregation of 16 June that decided the sentence; he was not at the abjuration.

occasions.label: Descartes tells Mersenne that, hearing of Galileo's condemnation, he will not publish Le Monde
The Discours de la méthode, with the Dioptrique, the Météores and the Géométrie; Mersenne handles it in Paris
Fermat's objections to the Dioptrique reach Descartes through Mersenne
occasions.note: Fermat had seen the Dioptrique in proof through Beaugrand; the months of the exchange are to be checked.

occasions.label: The dispute over Fermat's method of maxima and minima and of tangents, through Mersenne
Descartes writes to Fermat in conciliation, acknowledging his method
occasions.note: In letters to others Descartes went on disparaging Fermat.

occasions.label: Descartes to Mersenne on Galileo's Two New Sciences: he builds without foundations
The young Pascal's Essai pour les coniques; Descartes, sent it by Mersenne, judges that he learnt it from Desargues
The Meditationes with the Objections Mersenne collected, Hobbes's the third, and Descartes's dismissive Replies
Death of Galileo
Descartes visits Pascal; they disagree about the vacuum
occasions.note: Jacqueline Pascal's letter to her sister describes the two visits.

occasions.label: Death of Mersenne
Descartes arrives at the court of Queen Christina
occasions.note: Sweden kept the Julian calendar; the date is given New Style, as Descartes and his biographers give it.

occasions.label: Death of Descartes
occasions.note: 1 February 1650 in Sweden's Julian calendar.

occasions.label: The correspondence of Pascal and Fermat on the division of stakes
Wallis's Elenchus geometriae Hobbianae refutes Hobbes's squaring of the circle in De corpore
Hobbes's Six Lessons to the Professors of the Mathematiques, against Wallis
Hooke, Boyle's assistant, builds the air pump
After Wren's lecture at Gresham College, twelve men, Boyle among them, found a college for experimental learning
Hobbes's Dialogus physicus de natura aeris attacks Boyle's air pump and the new society
Oldenburg visits Spinoza and their correspondence begins
Spinoza's criticism of Boyle's experiments on nitre, sent through Oldenburg
occasions.note: The letter (Ep. 6) is undated; winter or spring 1662.

occasions.label: The first royal charter: the Royal Society, under the king's patronage, with Oldenburg one of its two secretaries
occasions.note: Oldenburg and Wilkins are named secretaries in the charters of 1662 and 1663; which first named them is to be checked.

occasions.label: Death of Pascal
Hooke, released from Boyle's service, made the Society's Curator of Experiments
Oldenburg sends Spinoza Boyle's answer on nitre
Hooke's Micrographia, printed with the Society's imprimatur
occasions.note: January 1664/5: January 1665 by the historical year, when Pepys bought his copy.

occasions.label: The first number of the Philosophical Transactions, Oldenburg's own venture
occasions.note: 6 March 1664/5: 1665 by the historical year.

occasions.label: The Académie royale des sciences first meets in the King's Library, Huygens its leading member
Barrow sends Newton's De analysi to Collins
Newton's letter on light and colours read to the Society
occasions.note: 8 February 1671/2; Newton had been elected a Fellow on 11 January 1671/2 after showing his reflecting telescope.

occasions.label: Hooke's critique of Newton's theory read to the Society and sent on by Oldenburg
Leibniz, newly in Paris, begins to learn mathematics under Huygens
Huygens's objections to Newton's theory of colours, sent through Oldenburg
Leibniz shows his calculating machine to the Royal Society; Hooke finds fault with it
occasions.note: Leibniz dated his letters New Style; the Society's minutes give the meeting Old Style.

occasions.label: After the objections to his theory, Newton asks Oldenburg to remove him from the Society
occasions.note: 8 March 1672/3. Oldenburg talked him round and the dues were waived.

occasions.label: Leibniz elected a Fellow of the Royal Society
Leibniz demonstrates his calculating machine before the Académie
Charles II's warrant makes Flamsteed his astronomical observator
Hooke's conciliatory letter and Newton's reply: if I have seen further it is by standing on the shoulders of giants
occasions.note: 20 January and 5 February 1675/6: 1676 by the historical year. Some read Newton's phrase as a gibe at Hooke's stature.

occasions.label: Newton's Epistola prior, for Leibniz, sent through Oldenburg: the binomial series
Leibniz, in London again, reads Newton's De analysi among Collins's papers and takes notes
occasions.note: The notes were turned against him in 1712.

occasions.label: Leibniz visits Spinoza and talks with him for days
Newton's Epistola posterior, through Oldenburg, hiding the method of fluxions in an anagram
occasions.note: 24 October 1676 Old Style is 3 November New Style; Leibniz received it only in 1677.

occasions.label: Death of Spinoza
Leibniz answers through Oldenburg, setting out his differential calculus
occasions.note: Dated New Style by Leibniz, though Hanover kept the Julian calendar until 1700. Newton did not reply.

occasions.label: Death of Oldenburg
Hooke, now secretary, reopens correspondence with Newton: the composition of orbital motion and the inverse square
occasions.note: 24 November 1679 to 17 January 1679/80. Hooke read Newton's mistaken spiral to the Society, and Newton broke off.

occasions.label: Death of Hobbes
Death of John Collins
Halley asks Newton what orbit an inverse-square force would give; an ellipse, Newton says, for he has calculated it
Death of Charles II
occasions.note: 6 February 1684/5.

occasions.label: Book I of the Principia before the Society; Hooke claims the inverse square, Halley reports it, Newton rages and strikes Hooke out
The Principia published at Halley's expense, with a scholium acknowledging Leibniz's method
occasions.note: The scholium to Book II, Lemma 2 was cut from the third edition of 1726.

occasions.label: Huygens in London meets Newton at the Royal Society and goes with him to recommend him to the king
Death of Boyle
Newton visits Flamsteed for lunar observations
Death of Huygens
The quarrel over the lunar observations: Newton wants Flamsteed's observations and not his calculations
Newton solves Johann Bernoulli's brachistochrone challenge in a night and answers anonymously
occasions.note: 29 January 1696/7, as Catherine Conduitt told it.

occasions.label: The solutions in the Acta Eruditorum; Bernoulli knows the anonymous English one, tanquam ex ungue leonem
